title: Acute ischaemic stroke: thrombolysis, thrombectomy & ASPECTS
subject: Medicine
anchor: Sudden focal deficit + a clear 'last known well' (LKW) time → stroke code: glucose first, then NCCT to exclude bleed
≤4.5 h from LKW → IV thrombolysis (TNK or alteplase) once BP <185/110
Large-vessel occlusion (ICA / M1) on CTA → mechanical thrombectomy up to 24 h (6–24 h needs perfusion/clinical-core mismatch)
algorithm:
Suspected stroke → ABC + capillary glucose (hypoglycaemia is the commonest mimic)
→ NCCT head (+ CTA for LVO; CTP/MRI if late or unknown onset)
  Haemorrhage → ICH pathway (no lysis)
  No haemorrhage →
    ≤4.5 h from LKW & no contraindication →
      BP ≥185/110 → IV labetalol / nicardipine first
      BP <185/110 → TNK 0.25 mg/kg single bolus (max 25 mg) OR alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg; 10% bolus over 1 min, rest over 60 min)
      After lysis: BP <180/105 for 24 h; no antiplatelet/anticoagulant for 24 h; repeat CT at 24 h
    Unknown onset / wake-up → MRI: DWI+ / FLAIR− mismatch → lysis eligible (WAKE-UP)
    LVO (ICA or M1) →
      0–6 h: pre-stroke mRS 0–1, NIHSS ≥6, ASPECTS ≥6 → thrombectomy (give IVT too if eligible; do not wait for response)
      6–24 h: DAWN (6–24 h) / DEFUSE-3 (6–16 h) mismatch → thrombectomy
    Not lysed → permissive BP up to 220/120; aspirin within 24–48 h
    Minor stroke (NIHSS ≤3) / high-risk TIA → aspirin + clopidogrel for 21 days

Regions
Note

Loss of insular ribbon & obscured lentiform = earliest CT signs

tables.title: IV thrombolytics in stroke
head: Feature
Tenecteplase (TNK)
Alteplase (rtPA)
rows: 10% IV bolus over 1 min, remaining 90% infused over 60 min
Do not use the cardiac (MI) weight-band dose

points: **Glucose first**: hypoglycaemia (<50 mg/dL) mimics stroke and must be corrected before lysis
Earliest CT signs: **hyperdense MCA sign** (thrombus), loss of insular ribbon, obscured lentiform nucleus, loss of grey–white differentiation
**DWI** MRI is the most sensitive test for acute infarct (positive within minutes); NCCT is the first test because its job is to exclude haemorrhage

Key lysis exclusions: any ICH on CT, ischaemic stroke/serious head trauma within 3 months, intracranial/spinal surgery within 3 months, GI bleed within 21 days, platelets <1,00,000, INR >1.7, aortic dissection, infective endocarditis, glucose <50 mg/dL
**sICH** after alteplase ≈ 6% (NINDS) – the main complication; also orolingual angioedema (more with ACE inhibitors)
**Bridging**: IVT and thrombectomy are given together – never delay groin puncture to watch the response to lysis
Thrombectomy 0–6 h criteria (AHA/ASA): age ≥18, pre-stroke mRS 0–1, ICA or M1 occlusion, NIHSS ≥6, ASPECTS ≥6
Post-lysis: BP <180/105 for 24 h, neuro checks, no antithrombotics for 24 h until repeat imaging excludes bleed
Minor non-cardioembolic stroke (NIHSS ≤3) or high-risk TIA (ABCD² ≥4): **DAPT 21 days** then single antiplatelet (CHANCE/POINT)

traps.stem: 64-year-old, left hemiparesis 2 h ago, NCCT no bleed, BP 195/115. Next step?
traps.trap: Start alteplase immediately because the patient is inside the 4.5 h window.
traps.fix: Lower BP first with IV labetalol or nicardipine to <185/110, then lyse. Lysis above this BP raises the risk of symptomatic ICH.

traps.stem: Terminal ICA occlusion at 2 h. IVT started. Wait to see if the deficit improves before calling interventional radiology?
traps.trap: Wait 60 min for the alteplase response – looks conservative.
traps.fix: Activate thrombectomy at once in parallel with IVT (bridging). IVT alone rarely recanalises an ICA/M1 clot.

traps.stem: Woke up with aphasia; LKW unknown. MRI: DWI-bright infarct, no FLAIR signal in that area.
traps.trap: Not eligible – onset unknown, so lysis is contraindicated.
traps.fix: DWI-positive/FLAIR-negative mismatch means the infarct is probably <4.5 h old → IV thrombolysis can be given (WAKE-UP trial).

cards.text: Acute stroke, BP 198/112, no bleed on CT: first lower BP to below {{c1::185/110 mmHg}} with IV labetalol/nicardipine; after lysis keep it below {{c2::180/105 mmHg}} for 24 h.
Tenecteplase dose in stroke is {{c1::0.25 mg/kg single bolus (max 25 mg)}}; alteplase is {{c2::0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg, 10% as bolus and the rest over 60 min}}.

cards.front: What does a DWI-positive / FLAIR-negative mismatch mean in a wake-up stroke?
cards.back: The infarct is likely <4.5 h old → patient is eligible for IV thrombolysis (WAKE-UP trial).

cards.front: Thrombectomy criteria in the 0–6 h window (AHA/ASA)?
cards.back: Age ≥18, pre-stroke mRS 0–1, causative ICA or M1 occlusion, NIHSS ≥6, ASPECTS ≥6. 6–24 h: DAWN/DEFUSE-3 mismatch selection.

cards.text: ASPECTS scores {{c1::10}} MCA regions on NCCT; a normal scan scores {{c2::10}} and each region with early ischaemic change subtracts 1.

cards.front: Untreated (not lysed) acute ischaemic stroke: when do you lower BP?
cards.back: Only if BP >220/120 mmHg (permissive hypertension protects the penumbra); then lower by about 15% in 24 h.

Diffusion-weighted MRI: acute infarct is bright (restricted diffusion) within minutes – the most sensitive imaging for early ischaemia

verify: AHA/ASA 2019 AIS guideline + TNK 0.25 mg/kg endorsement (2023–24); large-core trials (SELECT2, ANGEL-ASPECT 2023) now allow thrombectomy in selected ASPECTS 3–5 patients – exam-classic cut-off remains ASPECTS ≥6.

title: Status epilepticus: refractory & super-refractory escalation
subject: Medicine
anchor: Convulsive seizure ≥5 min, or ≥2 seizures without regaining consciousness between them = status epilepticus (t1 = 5 min)
Neuronal injury from t2 = 30 min → treat by the clock: benzodiazepine → one non-sedating IV ASM → anaesthetic infusion
Failing BZD + one second-line ASM = refractory; persisting ≥24 h after starting anaesthesia = super-refractory
algorithm:
0–5 min: ABC, O2, monitor, capillary glucose (hypoglycaemia → thiamine 100 mg IV then 50 mL of 50% dextrose)
5–20 min (Phase 1, benzodiazepine):
  IV access → lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (max 4 mg/dose), repeat once after 5–10 min
    or diazepam 0.15–0.2 mg/kg (max 10 mg/dose), repeat once
  No IV → IM midazolam 10 mg (>40 kg) / 5 mg (13–40 kg) (RAMPART); or intranasal/buccal midazolam, rectal diazepam
20–40 min (Phase 2, one non-sedating IV ASM):
  Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4500 mg) OR fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg (max 1500 mg PE) OR valproate 40 mg/kg (max 3000 mg)
  (phenobarbital 15–20 mg/kg if none available)
>40 min / still seizing → refractory SE (Phase 3):
  Intubate, ICU, continuous EEG
  Infusion: midazolam, propofol or thiopental/pentobarbital (± ketamine)
  Target: seizure suppression or burst suppression for 24–48 h, then slow wean
Recurs or persists ≥24 h after starting anaesthesia → super-refractory SE:
  Ketamine, ketogenic diet, immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, PLEX) for NORSE/FIRES, inhaled isoflurane, look for cause

tables.title: Second-line agents (ESETT: equal efficacy, about half stop seizing)
head: Drug
Loading dose (max)
Key caution
rows: Few interactions; safe in liver disease; renal dose adjust
20 mg PE/kg (1500 mg PE); ≤150 mg PE/min
Hypotension, arrhythmia – ECG monitoring; can be given IM
Propylene glycol vehicle → hypotension, bradyarrhythmia; purple glove syndrome; not IM
Avoid in liver disease, mitochondrial disease (POLG), pregnancy if possible; hyperammonaemia

points: **IV lorazepam** = drug of choice for initial treatment; **IM midazolam** is the choice without IV access (RAMPART: at least as effective as IV lorazepam pre-hospital)
Give a maximum of **two** benzodiazepine doses – further doses add respiratory depression without benefit
Benzodiazepine resistance develops because synaptic **GABA-A receptors are internalised** while NMDA/AMPA receptors move to the surface → rationale for **ketamine** (NMDA antagonist) in prolonged SE
**Fosphenytoin** is a water-soluble prodrug dosed in phenytoin equivalents (PE); can be infused 3× faster than phenytoin and given IM
**Propofol infusion syndrome**: metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia, cardiac failure – with high dose/prolonged infusion
Non-convulsive SE is a common cause of persistent coma after the convulsions stop → **EEG** is mandatory if the patient does not wake
Special causes: **eclampsia → MgSO₄**; **isoniazid toxicity → pyridoxine**; hypoglycaemia → dextrose; hyponatraemia → 3% saline

**NORSE** (new-onset refractory SE in a healthy person) – commonest identified cause autoimmune/paraneoplastic encephalitis (e.g., anti-NMDAR); **FIRES** = NORSE preceded by a febrile illness → early immunotherapy

traps.stem: Lorazepam 4 mg at 5 min, repeated at 12 min; still seizing at 22 min. Next?
traps.trap: A third lorazepam dose or rectal diazepam – 'one more try' with a benzodiazepine.
traps.fix: Escalate to a second-line IV ASM (levetiracetam, fosphenytoin or valproate). More than two BZD doses causes respiratory depression and does not work.

traps.stem: Why is fosphenytoin preferred over phenytoin for loading?
traps.trap: Because it is more effective at stopping seizures.
traps.fix: Efficacy is the same; fosphenytoin lacks the propylene glycol vehicle, can be given faster (≤150 mg PE/min vs ≤50 mg/min), causes less hypotension/tissue injury (no purple glove) and can be given IM.

traps.stem: Healthy 16-year-old, fever a week ago, now refractory SE with normal MRI.
traps.trap: Just keep adding anti-seizure drugs and anaesthetics.
traps.fix: Think NORSE/FIRES: send autoimmune encephalitis panel (anti-NMDAR etc.) and start early immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG/PLEX).

cards.text: Status epilepticus without IV access: first-line is {{c1::IM midazolam 10 mg (>40 kg)}}, supported by the {{c2::RAMPART}} trial.
Operational t1 for convulsive status epilepticus is {{c1::5 min}} and t2 (risk of neuronal injury) is {{c2::30 min}}.

cards.front: ESETT second-line loading doses?
cards.back: Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4500 mg); fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg (max 1500 mg PE); valproate 40 mg/kg (max 3000 mg). All roughly equally effective (~half respond).

cards.front: Definition of super-refractory status epilepticus?
cards.back: SE that continues or recurs ≥24 h after starting anaesthetic infusion, including recurrence on weaning.

cards.text: Benzodiazepines fail in prolonged SE because synaptic {{c1::GABA-A receptors are internalised}}, while {{c2::NMDA}} receptors are upregulated – hence ketamine.

cards.front: Maximum infusion rate: phenytoin vs fosphenytoin?
cards.back: Phenytoin ≤50 mg/min; fosphenytoin ≤150 mg PE/min (with cardiac monitoring for both).

verify: ILAE 2015 definitions; AES 2016 guideline + ESETT (2019); Neurocritical Care Society escalation.

title: Brainstem & vascular stroke localisation
subject: Medicine
anchor: Crossed signs = brainstem: IPSILATERAL cranial nerve + CONTRALATERAL long tract
Medial (paramedian) syndromes hit motor (pyramid/corticospinal), medial lemniscus, and the nerve that exits medially (III, VI, XII)
Lateral syndromes hit spinothalamic, sympathetic (Horner), trigeminal sensory, cerebellar peduncles, vestibular, IX/X – and spare power

tables.title: Classic brainstem syndromes
head: Syndrome
Site / artery
Ipsilateral
Contralateral
rows: Ventral midbrain (cerebral peduncle) / PCA paramedian branches
CN III palsy (down & out, ptosis, dilated pupil)
Dorsal midbrain tegmentum (red nucleus, superior cerebellar peduncle)
Bilateral: upgaze palsy, light–near dissociation, convergence–retraction nystagmus, lid retraction
CN VI (abduction) + CN VII (LMN face) palsy
Horizontal gaze palsy to side of lesion + CN VII palsy
Quadriplegia + anarthria; consciousness, vertical gaze and blinking preserved
Face pain/temp loss (spinal V), Horner, ataxia, dysphagia/hoarseness/↓gag (nucleus ambiguus), vertigo/nystagmus
Tongue deviates TO the lesion (CN XII)
Hemiplegia (arm & leg, face spared) + loss of vibration/position (medial lemniscus)

tables.title: Supratentorial & lacunar localisation
head: Lesion
Deficit
rows: Contralateral leg > arm, urinary incontinence, abulia, grasp reflex
Contralateral face & arm > leg weakness/sensory loss; Broca aphasia (dominant); eyes deviate TOWARD lesion
Wernicke aphasia (dominant) / neglect (non-dominant, usually right parietal); contralateral superior quadrantanopia
Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing; dominant PCA + splenium → alexia without agraphia
Pure motor hemiplegia face + arm + leg equally
Pure sensory stroke; later thalamic pain (Dejerine–Roussy)

points: **Lateral medullary syndrome**: commonest cause is **vertebral artery** occlusion (more than PICA itself); no limb weakness and no tongue involvement
**Medial medullary**: tongue deviates **towards** the lesion; hemiplegia is contralateral (pyramids decussate below)
**Weber** = III + contralateral hemiplegia; **Benedikt** = III + contralateral tremor/ataxia (red nucleus)
**Millard-Gubler** = VI + VII + contralateral hemiplegia; **Foville** adds a horizontal **gaze** palsy (PPRF/VI nucleus)
**Locked-in syndrome**: basilar occlusion with bilateral ventral pons infarct – communicate by vertical eye movement/blinking; EEG normal (not coma)
**AICA** (lateral pontine) syndrome = Wallenberg-like + ipsilateral facial palsy and **deafness** (labyrinthine artery)
**Gerstmann syndrome** (dominant angular gyrus): agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left–right disorientation
**Anton syndrome**: bilateral occipital (PCA) infarcts → cortical blindness with denial; pupils react normally
Lacunes = small deep infarcts from **lipohyalinosis** of penetrating arteries in hypertension/diabetes; no cortical signs (no aphasia, neglect, field cut)

traps.stem: Vertigo, hoarseness, right Horner, right facial and left body pain/temperature loss, normal power.
traps.trap: Medial medullary syndrome – because it is medullary.
traps.fix: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome – crossed pain/temperature loss + Horner + nucleus ambiguus signs and NO weakness; commonest culprit is the vertebral artery.

traps.stem: Tongue deviates to the right; left hemiparesis; left loss of joint position sense.
traps.trap: Left-sided lesion because the hemiparesis is on the left.
traps.fix: Right medial medullary syndrome: the tongue points TO the lesion (ipsilateral XII), long tract signs are contralateral.

traps.stem: Right gaze deviation in acute stroke with left hemiparesis.
traps.trap: Pontine lesion on the left (eyes look away from the lesion).
traps.fix: Hemispheric (frontal eye field) lesions push the eyes TOWARD the lesion (right MCA). Pontine lesions make the eyes look AWAY from the lesion, i.e. towards the hemiparesis.

cards.text: Weber syndrome: ipsilateral {{c1::CN III palsy}} + contralateral {{c2::hemiplegia}}; site {{c3::ventral midbrain (cerebral peduncle)}}.
In medial medullary syndrome the tongue deviates {{c1::towards}} the lesion and the limbs are weak on the {{c2::opposite}} side.

cards.front: Lateral medullary syndrome – what is NOT involved?
cards.back: Corticospinal tract (no weakness), medial lemniscus (vibration/position preserved) and CN XII (tongue normal).

cards.front: Millard-Gubler vs Foville syndrome?
cards.back: Both: ipsilateral VII + contralateral hemiplegia. Millard-Gubler (ventral pons) adds VI palsy (abduction); Foville (dorsal pons) adds conjugate horizontal gaze palsy to the lesion side.

cards.text: Alexia without agraphia = dominant {{c1::PCA}} infarct involving the occipital cortex and the {{c2::splenium of the corpus callosum}}.

cards.front: Pure motor hemiplegia (face, arm, leg equally, no cortical signs) – site and vessel?
cards.back: Posterior limb of internal capsule (or basis pontis); lenticulostriate branches of MCA – lacunar infarct.

title: Parkinsonism & movement disorders: PD vs MSA vs PSP vs DLB vs CBD
subject: Medicine
anchor: Asymmetric rest tremor + bradykinesia + rigidity + clear levodopa response = idiopathic Parkinson disease
'Parkinson-plus' red flags: early falls, early autonomic failure, vertical gaze palsy, early dementia/hallucinations, apraxia/alien limb, poor levodopa response
Chorea + psychiatric change + dementia + autosomal dominant with anticipation = Huntington (CAG repeat, caudate atrophy)

tables.title: Parkinsonian syndromes
head: Disorder
Key clinical clue
Imaging / pathology
Levodopa
rows: Asymmetric pill-rolling rest tremor, hyposmia, REM sleep behaviour disorder, constipation
Loss of substantia nigra pars compacta; Lewy bodies (α-synuclein)
Early severe autonomic failure (orthostatic hypotension, urinary, erectile), cerebellar signs, stridor, antecollis
'Hot cross bun' sign in pons; glial cytoplasmic inclusions (α-synuclein in oligodendrocytes)
Vertical (downgaze first) supranuclear gaze palsy, early backward falls, axial rigidity, retrocollis, surprised stare
Midbrain atrophy: 'hummingbird/penguin' sign, 'Mickey Mouse' sign; 4-repeat tau
Dementia before or within 1 year of parkinsonism, fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, RBD
Cortical Lewy bodies; reduced occipital metabolism
Very asymmetric rigidity, limb apraxia, alien limb, cortical sensory loss, myoclonus

tables.title: Drug-induced movement disorders (antipsychotics)
head: Reaction
Onset
Treatment
rows: Stop drug, cooling, dantrolene / bromocriptine; CK markedly ↑

points: **Huntington disease**: autosomal dominant **CAG** repeat in *HTT* (chromosome 4p); ≥40 repeats fully penetrant, 36–39 reduced penetrance; **anticipation** mainly with paternal transmission
HD pathology: loss of GABAergic medium spiny neurons of the **caudate** → 'box-car' lateral ventricles on imaging; chorea treated with **tetrabenazine**

**Wilson disease**: AR *ATP7B* (chromosome 13); low ceruloplasmin, ↑24-h urinary copper, **KF ring** (Descemet membrane) almost always present with neuro disease; wing-beating tremor, dystonia, 'face of the giant panda' on MRI midbrain
Wilson treatment: chelation (penicillamine, trientine) + zinc (blocks gut absorption); liver transplant for fulminant failure
**Levodopa + carbidopa** is the most effective PD drug; long-term problems = wearing-off, on–off, peak-dose dyskinesia
**DaT scan** (ioflupane SPECT) is reduced in PD/MSA/PSP/DLB but **normal in essential tremor and drug-induced parkinsonism**
**DLB**: avoid typical antipsychotics (life-threatening sensitivity); cholinesterase inhibitor (rivastigmine) helps cognition/hallucinations
**Essential tremor**: bilateral postural/action tremor, family history, improves with alcohol; treat propranolol or primidone
Deep brain stimulation targets: **STN** or GPi (PD), Vim thalamus (essential tremor)

traps.stem: Parkinsonism with frequent backward falls in year 1 and inability to look down.
traps.trap: Idiopathic PD with postural instability.
traps.fix: PSP – early falls + vertical (especially downward) supranuclear gaze palsy; postural instability appears late in PD.

traps.stem: Parkinsonism with marked orthostatic hypotension, urinary incontinence and poor levodopa response; pons shows a cross-shaped hyperintensity.
traps.trap: PD with autonomic dysfunction (PD can have dysautonomia).
traps.fix: MSA – early severe autonomic failure, poor levodopa response and the 'hot cross bun' sign; inclusions are in oligodendroglia (glial cytoplasmic inclusions).

traps.stem: Elderly patient with visual hallucinations and fluctuating cognition becomes rigid and confused after haloperidol.
traps.trap: Delirium – give more haloperidol.
traps.fix: Dementia with Lewy bodies with neuroleptic sensitivity – avoid typical antipsychotics; use rivastigmine (quetiapine/clozapine if an antipsychotic is unavoidable).

cards.text: Huntington disease: {{c1::CAG}} trinucleotide repeat in the HTT gene on chromosome {{c2::4}}; atrophy of the {{c3::caudate nucleus}}.

cards.front: MSA vs PD – inclusion body location?
cards.back: Both α-synuclein. PD: Lewy bodies in neurons. MSA: glial cytoplasmic inclusions in oligodendrocytes (Papp–Lantos).

cards.text: PSP: supranuclear gaze palsy affecting {{c1::vertical (downward first)}} gaze; MRI {{c2::hummingbird}} sign from midbrain atrophy; protein {{c3::4-repeat tau}}.

cards.front: Which antipsychotic side-effect appears after months–years and what treats it?
cards.back: Tardive dyskinesia – switch to clozapine/stop offending drug; VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine, tetrabenazine).

cards.front: DaT scan normal in a tremulous patient – what are the options?
cards.back: Essential tremor, drug-induced parkinsonism, psychogenic tremor (normal presynaptic dopamine terminals).

cards.text: Wilson disease gene {{c1::ATP7B}} on chromosome 13; serum ceruloplasmin is {{c2::low}} and 24-h urinary copper is {{c3::high}}.

verify: Harrison 21e; MDS clinical diagnostic criteria for PD (2015); DLB consortium 2017.

title: MS vs NMOSD/MOGAD vs GBS vs myasthenia gravis
subject: Medicine
anchor: Young woman, episodes separated in time and space: optic neuritis, INO, Lhermitte, Uhthoff → MS (periventricular 'Dawson fingers', CSF oligoclonal bands)
Severe optic neuritis + longitudinally extensive myelitis (≥3 segments) + intractable hiccups/vomiting → NMOSD (anti-AQP4)
Ascending flaccid weakness with areflexia after diarrhoea → GBS; fatigable ptosis/diplopia, normal reflexes and sensation → myasthenia

tables.title: Central demyelination: MS vs NMOSD vs MOGAD
head: Feature
MS
NMOSD (AQP4+)
MOGAD
rows: Periventricular ovoid lesions perpendicular to ventricles (Dawson fingers), juxtacortical, infratentorial
Usually absent; neutrophils may be present
Interferon-β, glatiramer, ocrelizumab, natalizumab, fingolimod, etc.
Rituximab, eculizumab, inebilizumab, satralizumab; interferon-β may worsen

tables.title: Peripheral: GBS vs myasthenia gravis vs LEMS
head: Feature
GBS (AIDP)
Myasthenia gravis
LEMS
rows: Ascending, symmetric, flaccid; may involve respiratory & facial muscles
Proximal legs; improves briefly with use
AChR antibodies; decremental RNS; single-fibre EMG
IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day × 5 d or PLEX; steroids NOT useful
Pyridostigmine, steroids, immunosuppressants, thymectomy; crisis → IVIG/PLEX
3,4-diaminopyridine; search for small cell lung cancer

points: **McDonald 2017**: dissemination in space = T2 lesions in ≥2 of 4 areas (periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord); time = new/enhancing + non-enhancing lesions or new lesion on follow-up; **CSF-specific OCB can substitute for dissemination in time**; symptomatic lesions now count
MS clinical clues: **INO** (MLF lesion – adducting eye fails, abducting eye nystagmus), **Lhermitte** sign, **Uhthoff** (worse with heat), painful optic neuritis with RAPD
MS relapse: **IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3–5 days**; PLEX if steroid-refractory. Ocrelizumab is the first drug approved for **primary progressive MS**
Natalizumab → **PML** (JC virus); fingolimod → first-dose bradycardia, macular oedema
**NMOSD** core: optic neuritis, LETM, **area postrema syndrome** (intractable hiccups/vomiting); acute attacks need steroids + early PLEX
**GBS**: commonest preceding infection *Campylobacter jejuni* (AMAN, anti-GM1); CSF high protein with **<10 cells/µL** (may be normal in week 1)
GBS ventilation trigger: **FVC <20 mL/kg**, MIP weaker than −30 cmH₂O or MEP <40 cmH₂O ('20/30/40 rule'); single-breath count is a bedside screen
**Miller Fisher**: ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia – **anti-GQ1b**; CIDP = progression >8 weeks, steroid-responsive
**Myasthenia**: anti-AChR (~85% generalised), anti-MuSK (bulbar, women, poor pyridostigmine response), thymoma in ~10–15% (CT chest in all); ice-pack test improves ptosis
MG worsened by aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, magnesium, β-blockers, neuromuscular blockers; **thymectomy** benefits AChR+ generalised MG (MGTX)

traps.stem: GBS patient, day 3: CSF protein normal, cells 2/µL.
traps.trap: Normal CSF excludes GBS.
traps.fix: Albuminocytological dissociation may take 1–2 weeks to appear; diagnosis is clinical + nerve conduction. Treat with IVIG/PLEX without waiting.

traps.stem: GBS with severe weakness – add IV methylprednisolone?
traps.trap: Steroids, as for most autoimmune neurological diseases.
traps.fix: Corticosteroids are of no benefit in GBS (alone or with IVIG). Treat with IVIG or plasma exchange (not combined sequentially).

traps.stem: Myasthenic patient on pyridostigmine becomes weak with fasciculations, miosis, salivation and diarrhoea.
traps.trap: Myasthenic crisis – increase pyridostigmine.
traps.fix: Cholinergic crisis from excess anticholinesterase → stop pyridostigmine, support ventilation, atropine for muscarinic effects. (Muscarinic signs point to cholinergic crisis.)

cards.text: NMOSD antibody targets {{c1::aquaporin-4}} on {{c2::astrocytes}}; spinal lesion spans ≥{{c3::3}} vertebral segments.
In McDonald 2017, CSF-specific {{c1::oligoclonal bands}} can substitute for dissemination in {{c2::time}}.

cards.front: Dawson fingers – what and where?
cards.back: Ovoid periventricular demyelinating plaques oriented perpendicular to the lateral ventricles (along medullary veins), best on sagittal FLAIR – classic MS.

cards.text: GBS CSF: {{c1::raised protein}} with {{c2::normal cell count}} = albuminocytological dissociation.

cards.front: Repetitive nerve stimulation: myasthenia vs LEMS?
cards.back: MG: decremental response at low-rate (2–3 Hz). LEMS: low CMAP that increments >100% after exercise/high-rate stimulation.

cards.front: Miller Fisher syndrome antibody and triad?
cards.back: Anti-GQ1b; ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia.

title: Intracerebral & subarachnoid haemorrhage
subject: Medicine
anchor: Thunderclap 'worst headache of life' peaking within a minute ± neck stiffness, collapse → SAH until proven otherwise
NCCT first; if negative and clinical suspicion stays high → LP for xanthochromia (≥12 h after onset)
Hypertensive elderly with sudden deficit + headache/vomiting/↓GCS → ICH (putamen commonest); lobar bleed in the elderly → amyloid angiopathy
algorithm:
Thunderclap headache → NCCT head
  Blood in basal cisterns/sylvian fissures → SAH → CTA (DSA = gold standard) to find aneurysm
  NCCT negative → LP (ideally ≥12 h after onset) → xanthochromia / non-clearing RBCs → CTA
Confirmed aneurysmal SAH →
  Grade: Hunt & Hess / WFNS; modified Fisher for vasospasm risk
  Nimodipine 60 mg orally every 4 h for 21 days
  Control BP (commonly SBP <160) until aneurysm secured; reverse anticoagulants
  Secure aneurysm early (within 24–72 h): endovascular coiling if feasible, else clipping
  Hydrocephalus → external ventricular drain
  Days 3–14: watch for delayed cerebral ischaemia (vasospasm) → TCD; keep euvolaemia; induced hypertension if DCI
  Hyponatraemia → cerebral salt wasting (do NOT fluid restrict) vs SIADH

Elderly; cortical microbleeds & superficial siderosis on gradient-echo MRI (Boston criteria)

points: Commonest cause of SAH overall = **trauma**; of spontaneous SAH = **ruptured saccular (berry) aneurysm** (~80–85%)
Commonest aneurysm site: **anterior communicating artery**; **posterior communicating artery** aneurysm → pupil-involving CN III palsy
Berry aneurysm associations: **ADPKD**, Ehlers–Danlos type IV, Marfan, coarctation of aorta, smoking, hypertension
NCCT sensitivity for SAH is highest in the first 6 h and falls over days; **xanthochromia** (bilirubin from RBC breakdown) needs ~12 h to develop
**Nimodipine** 60 mg q4h × 21 days improves outcome (neuroprotection) – it does not reliably prevent angiographic vasospasm
**Rebleeding** risk is highest in the first 24 h; **vasospasm** begins ~day 3, peaks days 7–10, resolves by ~day 14–21
Triple-H therapy is obsolete → maintain **euvolaemia**; induced hypertension for symptomatic DCI

Anticoagulant reversal: warfarin → **4-factor PCC + IV vitamin K**; dabigatran → **idarucizumab**; factor Xa inhibitors → **andexanet alfa** (or PCC)
**Cerebellar haemorrhage >3 cm** or with brainstem compression/hydrocephalus → urgent surgical evacuation; CTA **spot sign** predicts haematoma expansion

traps.stem: Sudden severe headache 8 h ago, NCCT normal, neck mildly stiff.
traps.trap: Normal CT rules out SAH – discharge with analgesics.
traps.fix: CT sensitivity falls with time; perform LP (≥12 h after onset) for xanthochromia, or CTA, before excluding SAH.

traps.stem: Day 6 after aneurysmal SAH: new confusion and hemiparesis, CT shows no rebleed.
traps.trap: Rebleeding – rebleed is the commonest early complication.
traps.fix: Delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm (peak days 7–10; window 3–14): continue nimodipine, keep euvolaemia, induced hypertension, consider endovascular therapy.

traps.stem: SAH patient with Na 126 mmol/L, dehydrated, high urine output.
traps.trap: SIADH → fluid restriction.
traps.fix: Cerebral salt wasting (hypovolaemic) – give isotonic/hypertonic saline (± fludrocortisone). Fluid restriction risks vasospasm-related infarction.

cards.text: Commonest site of berry aneurysm: {{c1::anterior communicating artery}}; aneurysm causing pupil-involving third nerve palsy: {{c2::posterior communicating artery}}.
After aneurysmal SAH, vasospasm starts around day {{c1::3}}, peaks at days {{c2::7–10}}; prevention of poor outcome uses {{c3::nimodipine 60 mg every 4 h for 21 days}}.

cards.front: CT-negative suspected SAH – what is the next test and when?
cards.back: Lumbar puncture ≥12 h after headache onset for xanthochromia (spectrophotometry) and RBC count; or CTA.

cards.front: Modified Fisher grade 4?
cards.back: Thick cisternal SAH with intraventricular haemorrhage – highest risk of vasospasm/delayed cerebral ischaemia.

cards.front: Commonest site of hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage and its vascular lesion?
cards.back: Putamen (basal ganglia) – rupture of lenticulostriate penetrating arteries with Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms/lipohyalinosis.

cards.front: Warfarin-associated ICH reversal?
cards.back: Stop warfarin; 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate + IV vitamin K 10 mg (FFP if PCC unavailable).

title: Acute coronary syndrome: STEMI vs NSTEMI, reperfusion & complications
subject: Medicine
anchor: Ischaemic chest pain + new ST elevation in 2 contiguous leads (or STEMI equivalent) → reperfusion now: primary PCI ≤90 min (≤120 min if transfer), else lysis within 30 min
Chest pain + troponin rise/fall without ST elevation → NSTEMI: risk stratify (GRACE/TIMI), DAPT + anticoagulant, invasive strategy by risk; never thrombolyse
New murmur/shock days 3–7 after MI → mechanical complication (papillary muscle rupture, VSR, free-wall rupture)
algorithm:
Chest pain → 12-lead ECG within 10 min of first medical contact (FMC)
  STEMI (or new LBBB with Sgarbossa / posterior MI / de Winter) →
    Aspirin 150–325 mg chewed + P2Y12 (ticagrelor 180 / prasugrel 60 / clopidogrel 600 mg) + UFH
    PCI-capable centre → primary PCI, FMC-to-device ≤90 min
    Non-PCI centre: if FMC-to-device would exceed 120 min → fibrinolysis, door-to-needle ≤30 min (within 12 h of symptoms)
      → transfer for angiography 2–24 h (pharmaco-invasive)
      → failed lysis (<50% ST resolution at 60–90 min, ongoing pain) → rescue PCI
  No ST elevation → serial hs-troponin (0/1 h or 0/2 h)
    Very high risk (shock, refractory pain, VT/VF, mechanical complication, acute HF, recurrent dynamic ST change) → angiography <2 h
    High risk (NSTEMI confirmed, GRACE >140, dynamic ST/T) → angiography <24 h
    Low risk → selective invasive / stress testing
All: high-intensity statin, β-blocker (if no HF/shock), ACEi/ARB, DAPT 12 months

Persistent STE weeks after anterior MI; fever + pericarditis weeks later

points: STEMI ECG: new STE at J point in 2 contiguous leads ≥1 mm (all leads except V2–V3); V2–V3 ≥2 mm men ≥40 y, ≥2.5 mm men <40 y, ≥1.5 mm women

**Absolute contraindications to fibrinolysis**: any prior ICH; known cerebral vascular lesion (AVM) or malignant intracranial neoplasm; ischaemic stroke within 3 months; suspected aortic dissection; active bleeding/bleeding diathesis (not menses); significant closed head/facial trauma within 3 months; intracranial/spinal surgery within 2 months
Relative contraindications: BP >180/110 at presentation, traumatic/prolonged CPR, pregnancy, active peptic ulcer, oral anticoagulant, prior streptokinase (for streptokinase)
**Troponin**: rises 3–4 h (hs-troponin earlier), stays raised 7–14 days; **CK-MB** normalises by 48–72 h → useful for reinfarction
**RV infarct** (inferior STEMI + hypotension + clear lungs + raised JVP): give fluids, avoid nitrates/diuretics/morphine
**Wellens** pattern (deep or biphasic T in V2–V3, pain-free) = critical proximal LAD stenosis → angiography, avoid stress testing

**TIMI** score for UA/NSTEMI (7 items, 1 point each): age ≥65, ≥3 CAD risk factors, known CAD (stenosis ≥50%), aspirin in last 7 days, ≥2 anginal episodes in 24 h, ST deviation ≥0.5 mm, positive marker. **GRACE** predicts mortality best and guides timing of angiography
**Killip** class: I no HF; II rales/S3; III pulmonary oedema; IV cardiogenic shock
Oxygen only if SpO₂ <90%; nitrates contraindicated with PDE-5 inhibitor use (sildenafil within 24 h, tadalafil within 48 h)
Histology timeline (Robbins): neutrophils 1–3 days; macrophages & maximal softening 3–7 days (rupture window); granulation tissue from ~7–10 days; dense scar by ~2 months

traps.stem: Inferior STEMI, BP 80/50, clear lungs, raised JVP. Next drug?
traps.trap: Sublingual nitroglycerine for the chest pain.
traps.fix: RV infarction is preload-dependent: give IV fluids and avoid nitrates/diuretics; reperfuse urgently (check V4R).

traps.stem: NSTEMI patient, troponin positive, ongoing mild pain, nearest cath lab 3 h away. Thrombolyse?
traps.trap: Yes – thrombolysis for any MI when PCI is delayed.
traps.fix: Fibrinolysis has no benefit (and is harmful) in NSTE-ACS. Give DAPT + anticoagulant and arrange early invasive strategy.

traps.stem: Day 5 after anterior MI: sudden hypotension, new pansystolic murmur at left sternal edge, no pulmonary oedema initially; RV saturation higher than RA.
traps.trap: Papillary muscle rupture – both give a new pansystolic murmur.
traps.fix: Ventricular septal rupture: oxygen step-up from RA to RV on right-heart catheter. Papillary muscle rupture gives acute MR (apical murmur, pulmonary oedema, large v waves in PCWP).

cards.text: STEMI reperfusion targets: door/FMC-to-device ≤{{c1::90 min}} for primary PCI; door-to-needle ≤{{c2::30 min}} for fibrinolysis.
Inferior wall MI shows ST elevation in {{c1::II, III, aVF}} and is usually due to the {{c2::right coronary artery}}.

cards.front: Posterior MI ECG?
cards.back: ST depression with tall broad R waves and upright T in V1–V3 (mirror image); confirm with ST elevation in V7–V9.

cards.front: Free-wall rupture after MI – timing and presentation?
cards.back: Typically days 3–7 (macrophage/softening phase): sudden haemopericardium → tamponade → PEA arrest.

cards.text: CK-MB returns to normal in {{c1::48–72 h}}, so it is used to detect {{c2::reinfarction}}; troponin stays raised for 7–14 days.

cards.front: Persistent ST elevation 4 weeks after anterior MI?
cards.back: Left ventricular aneurysm (dyskinetic scar) – risk of mural thrombus, HF and ventricular arrhythmia.

title: ACLS: cardiac arrest, tachycardia & bradycardia algorithms
subject: Medicine
anchor: Pulseless → CPR 30:2, 100–120/min, 5–6 cm; check rhythm: shockable (VF/pVT) → shock first; non-shockable (PEA/asystole) → adrenaline first
Pulse + tachycardia: UNSTABLE (hypotension, altered mentation, shock, ischaemic chest pain, acute HF) → synchronised cardioversion
Stable regular narrow-complex → vagal manoeuvre → adenosine 6 mg rapid push, then 12 mg
algorithm:
Cardiac arrest → start CPR, attach defibrillator
  VF / pulseless VT →
    Shock (biphasic 120–200 J per device; monophasic 360 J) → CPR 2 min
    Shock → CPR + adrenaline 1 mg IV/IO, repeat every 3–5 min
    Shock → CPR + amiodarone 300 mg (2nd dose 150 mg) or lidocaine 1–1.5 mg/kg (then 0.5–0.75 mg/kg)
  PEA / asystole →
    CPR + adrenaline 1 mg as soon as possible, every 3–5 min
    No shock, no atropine; search & treat H's and T's
  Advanced airway → 1 breath every 6 s with continuous compressions; waveform capnography
Tachycardia with pulse →
  Unstable → synchronised cardioversion (narrow regular 50–100 J; narrow irregular/AF 120–200 J; wide regular 100 J)
  Polymorphic VT → unsynchronised defibrillation (torsades → MgSO4 2 g IV)
  Stable narrow regular → vagal manoeuvres → adenosine 6 mg → 12 mg → β-blocker / diltiazem
  Stable wide regular → adenosine only if regular & monomorphic → procainamide / amiodarone 150 mg over 10 min / sotalol
Bradycardia with poor perfusion →
  Atropine 1 mg IV every 3–5 min (max 3 mg)
  → ineffective: transcutaneous pacing OR dopamine 5–20 µg/kg/min OR adrenaline 2–10 µg/min → transvenous pacing

tables.title: Energy & drug doses (adult)
head: Situation
Dose
rows: Biphasic 120–200 J (device-specific; use maximum if unknown); monophasic 360 J
6 mg rapid IV push + saline flush, then 12 mg
2 J/kg, then 4 J/kg, subsequent ≥4 J/kg (max 10 J/kg)

points: High-quality CPR: rate **100–120/min**, depth **5–6 cm**, full recoil, interruptions <10 s, compression fraction ≥60% (aim 80%)
Shockable rhythm: adrenaline after the **2nd** shock; amiodarone after the **3rd** shock. Non-shockable: adrenaline **immediately**
Atropine is **not** used in PEA/asystole (removed 2010). Bradycardia atropine dose raised to **1 mg** (2020)
**ETCO₂** <10 mmHg after 20 min of CPR suggests poor prognosis; an abrupt rise to ≥35–40 mmHg suggests **ROSC**
Atropine fails in **Mobitz II / complete heart block with wide QRS** and in transplanted hearts → pace
Adenosine: halve dose (3 mg) via central line, with dipyridamole/carbamazepine, or in heart transplant; larger dose needed with theophylline/caffeine; avoid in severe asthma

**WPW + AF** (irregular, very fast, wide/variable QRS): **avoid AV-nodal blockers** (adenosine, β-blocker, verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin; IV amiodarone also discouraged) → procainamide/ibutilide or synchronised cardioversion; definitive = accessory-pathway ablation
WPW ECG: short PR (<120 ms), **delta wave**, wide QRS; orthodromic AVRT (narrow) is the commonest tachycardia in WPW
Post-ROSC: SpO₂ 92–98%, PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg, MAP ≥65, temperature control 32–37.5 °C and avoid fever; emergent angiography if STEMI
**Torsades de pointes**: IV magnesium sulfate 2 g; correct K⁺/Mg²⁺; overdrive pacing or isoprenaline; stop QT-prolonging drugs

traps.stem: Irregular wide-complex tachycardia at 240/min with varying QRS morphology in a young man with known WPW; BP 110/70.
traps.trap: IV adenosine or verapamil to slow the rate.
traps.fix: Pre-excited AF: AV-nodal blockade drives conduction down the accessory pathway → VF. Use procainamide or ibutilide (or synchronised cardioversion if unstable).

traps.stem: Asystole on the monitor during arrest.
traps.trap: Defibrillate (or give atropine).
traps.fix: Asystole is non-shockable: CPR + adrenaline 1 mg every 3–5 min, look for H's & T's. Confirm asystole in two leads/gain (fine VF can mimic it).

traps.stem: Narrow-complex regular tachycardia 180/min, BP 70/40, confused.
traps.trap: Adenosine 6 mg because the rhythm is SVT.
traps.fix: Unstable tachycardia → synchronised cardioversion (50–100 J) without delay; adenosine may be tried only if it does not delay cardioversion.

cards.text: In VF arrest adrenaline 1 mg is given after the {{c1::second}} shock and amiodarone {{c2::300 mg}} after the {{c3::third}} shock.
Stable SVT: adenosine {{c1::6 mg}} rapid IV push, then {{c2::12 mg}} if no response.

cards.front: Bradycardia with hypotension – first drug and dose? If it fails?
cards.back: Atropine 1 mg IV every 3–5 min (max 3 mg). Then transcutaneous pacing or dopamine 5–20 µg/kg/min / adrenaline 2–10 µg/min infusion.

cards.front: Synchronised cardioversion energy: narrow regular vs AF?
cards.back: Narrow regular (SVT, flutter): 50–100 J. AF: 120–200 J biphasic. Monomorphic VT with pulse: 100 J.

cards.front: Why avoid AV-nodal blockers in pre-excited AF (WPW)?
cards.back: Blocking the AV node lets all impulses pass via the accessory pathway (no decremental conduction) → very fast ventricular rate → VF.

cards.text: Compression rate {{c1::100–120/min}}, depth {{c2::5–6 cm}}, ratio {{c3::30:2}} without an advanced airway.

images.caption: WPW: short PR interval with slurred upstroke of QRS (delta wave) and wide QRS – in AF this pathway allows dangerously fast conduction

subject: Medicine
anchor: Dyspnoea, orthopnoea, PND, raised JVP, S3, basal crackles, oedema + raised BNP → heart failure; echo EF classifies it
HFrEF mortality benefit = four pillars: ARNI/ACEi/ARB, β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor
Systolic murmur louder with Valsalva/standing and softer with squatting/handgrip = HOCM (or MVP); AS does the opposite

head: Criteria
Low-risk population
Moderate/high-risk population (e.g. India)
rows: Carditis (clinical or subclinical on echo), polyarthritis only, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules
Carditis (clinical/subclinical), monoarthritis OR polyarthritis OR polyarthralgia, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules
Polyarthralgia, fever ≥38.5 °C, ESR ≥60 mm/h and/or CRP ≥3.0 mg/dL, prolonged PR (unless carditis)
Monoarthralgia, fever ≥38 °C, ESR ≥30 mm/h and/or CRP ≥3.0 mg/dL, prolonged PR (unless carditis)
Initial ARF: 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor. Recurrent ARF: 2 major, 1 major + 2 minor, or 3 minor
Same rule; chorea alone or indolent carditis alone may suffice

points: **Framingham**: HF = 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor. Major: PND, neck vein distension, crackles, cardiomegaly, acute pulmonary oedema, S3, hepatojugular reflux, ↑JVP. Minor: ankle oedema, nocturnal cough, exertional dyspnoea, hepatomegaly, pleural effusion, tachycardia ≥120, vital capacity ↓ by ⅓
**BNP** <100 pg/mL or **NT-proBNP** <300 pg/mL makes acute HF unlikely; BNP is falsely low in obesity, high in renal failure/age; sacubitril raises BNP but not NT-proBNP
EF classes: **HFrEF ≤40%**, HFmrEF 41–49%, **HFpEF ≥50%**; SGLT2 inhibitors also benefit HFpEF

Other HFrEF tools: ivabradine (sinus HR ≥70), hydralazine + nitrate, digoxin (symptoms only), ICD if EF ≤35% despite ≥3 months GDMT, **CRT** if EF ≤35% + LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms; diuretics relieve congestion but do not reduce mortality

**Aortic stenosis**: ejection systolic murmur radiating to carotids, slow-rising pulse, soft A2; severe = Vmax ≥4 m/s, mean gradient ≥40 mmHg, AVA <1.0 cm²; symptoms (angina, syncope, HF) = valve replacement

**HOCM**: asymmetric septal hypertrophy, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, bisferiens pulse; commonest cause of sudden death in young athletes; avoid nitrates, diuretics, digoxin; β-blocker, mavacamten
**Mitral stenosis**: loud S1, opening snap, mid-diastolic rumble with presystolic accentuation (lost in AF); shorter S2–OS gap = more severe

**Modified Duke**: definite IE = 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor; possible = 1 major + 1 minor, or 3 minor. Major = typical organism in 2 separate blood cultures (or persistent bacteraemia, Coxiella phase I IgG >1:800) + endocardial involvement on echo

IE organisms: **S. aureus** commonest overall & IV drug users (tricuspid); viridans streptococci after dental work (subacute); **S. gallolyticus (bovis)** → colonoscopy for colon cancer; coagulase-negative staph in early prosthetic valve IE

**RHD secondary prophylaxis**: benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million units IM every 3–4 weeks (3-weekly in India); no carditis → 5 years or till age 21; carditis without residual disease → 10 years or till 21; residual valve disease → 10 years or till 40 (often lifelong)

traps.stem: Young athlete with systolic murmur that becomes louder on standing up from squatting.
traps.trap: Aortic stenosis – both are ejection systolic murmurs.
traps.fix: HOCM: ↓ preload (standing/Valsalva) increases LVOT obstruction and the murmur; AS murmur softens with ↓ preload.

traps.stem: Child in India with fever, monoarthritis of the knee, ESR 40, high ASO, prolonged PR.
traps.trap: Not ARF – Jones needs polyarthritis and ESR ≥60.
traps.fix: India is a moderate/high-risk population: monoarthritis counts as major; fever ≥38 °C, ESR ≥30 and prolonged PR count as minor → meets criteria.

traps.stem: HFrEF patient with leg oedema: which drug class improves survival – furosemide?
traps.trap: Loop diuretics, because they relieve congestion fastest.
traps.fix: Diuretics only relieve symptoms. Survival benefit: ARNI/ACEi/ARB, β-blocker (carvedilol, bisoprolol, metoprolol succinate), MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor.

cards.text: The four pillars of HFrEF therapy: {{c1::ARNI/ACEi/ARB}}, {{c2::β-blocker}}, {{c3::MRA}} and {{c4::SGLT2 inhibitor}}.
Framingham heart failure diagnosis requires {{c1::2 major}} or {{c2::1 major + 2 minor}} criteria.

cards.front: Modified Duke – definite IE?
cards.back: 2 major; or 1 major + 3 minor; or 5 minor.

cards.front: S. gallolyticus (bovis) endocarditis – what next?
cards.back: Colonoscopy – strong association with colorectal neoplasia.

cards.text: Jones 2015 in moderate/high-risk populations: monoarthritis or {{c1::polyarthralgia}} counts as a major criterion; ESR ≥{{c2::30}} mm/h is a minor criterion.

cards.front: Severe aortic stenosis echo thresholds?
cards.back: Peak velocity ≥4 m/s, mean gradient ≥40 mmHg, valve area <1.0 cm² (indexed <0.6 cm²/m²).

title: ARDS, lung-protective ventilation, COPD exacerbation & ABG oxygen indices
subject: Medicine
anchor: Within 1 week of an insult (sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration, pancreatitis, trauma, transfusion) → bilateral opacities + hypoxaemia not explained by heart failure = ARDS
Grade by PaO₂/FiO₂ on PEEP ≥5: mild 200–300, moderate 100–200, severe ≤100
Ventilate gently: VT 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, plateau ≤30 cmH₂O, adequate PEEP, prone if P/F <150

Hypoxaemic respiratory failure with bilateral infiltrates →
  Exclude cardiogenic oedema (echo, BNP) → ARDS (Berlin)
  Intubate if failing → volume-control ventilation
    VT 6 mL/kg PBW (range 4–8) → check plateau pressure ≤30 cmH₂O (driving pressure ideally <15)
    PEEP/FiO₂ table (higher PEEP for moderate–severe); target SpO₂ 88–95% / PaO₂ 55–80 mmHg
    Accept permissive hypercapnia (pH ≥7.20–7.25)
  P/F <150 → prone position ≥12–16 h/day (PROSEVA) ± short neuromuscular blockade
  Refractory → VV-ECMO
  Conservative fluids once shock resolved; treat the cause
COPD exacerbation → controlled O₂ to SpO₂ 88–92%, bronchodilators, prednisolone 40 mg × 5 days, antibiotics if purulent sputum
  pH ≤7.35 and PaCO₂ >45 mmHg despite therapy → NIV (BiPAP)
  NIV contraindicated / fails (worsening pH, GCS falling, arrest, can't protect airway, haemodynamic instability) → intubate

head: Pattern
Meaning
Causes
rows: Bronchospasm, secretions/mucus plug, kinked/bitten tube, small ETT
Pneumothorax, ARDS/pulmonary oedema, right mainstem intubation, atelectasis, abdominal distension, auto-PEEP

tables.title: Hypoxaemia mechanisms
head: Mechanism
A–a gradient
Corrects with 100% O₂?
Example
rows: ARDS, lobar consolidation, intracardiac R→L shunt

points: **Berlin 2012**: timing ≤1 week; bilateral opacities not explained by effusion/collapse/nodules; not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload; PaO₂/FiO₂ measured with PEEP ≥5 cmH₂O
Exam-classic (AECC 1994) used PCWP ≤18 mmHg and 'ALI' for P/F ≤300 – both dropped in Berlin; 2023 global definition allows SpO₂/FiO₂ ≤315 and high-flow nasal oxygen ≥30 L/min
**Predicted body weight**: men = 50 + 0.91 × (height cm − 152.4); women = 45.5 + 0.91 × (height cm − 152.4)
Pathology: **diffuse alveolar damage** with **hyaline membranes** (exudative phase) → type II pneumocyte proliferation → fibrosis
Alveolar gas equation: PAO₂ = FiO₂ × (760 − 47) − PaCO₂/0.8 (≈150 − 1.25 × PaCO₂ on room air at sea level); normal A–a gradient ≈ age/4 + 4 mmHg
**NIV indication in COPD**: acute hypercapnic respiratory acidosis (pH ≤7.35, PaCO₂ >45 mmHg); strongest evidence of benefit (↓ intubation & mortality)

NIV contraindications: respiratory arrest, haemodynamic instability, unable to protect airway/copious secretions, facial trauma/burns, recent upper GI/facial surgery, undrained pneumothorax, uncooperative
**Auto-PEEP** in COPD/asthma on ventilator → hypotension: disconnect briefly, reduce RR, shorten inspiratory time
Modes: **assist-control (VC)** delivers set VT for every breath; **pressure support** = patient-triggered, used for weaning; **SIMV** mixes mandatory and spontaneous breaths
Weaning: spontaneous breathing trial 30–120 min; **RSBI (f/VT in litres) <105** predicts successful extubation

traps.stem: ARDS patient: VT 500 mL (8.5 mL/kg actual weight) for a 165 cm, 85 kg man; plateau 34 cmH₂O.
traps.trap: Tidal volume is fine because it is <10 mL/kg of actual weight.
traps.fix: Use predicted body weight (~61 kg) → target ~370 mL (6 mL/kg PBW) and plateau ≤30 cmH₂O.

traps.stem: COPD exacerbation, SpO₂ 82% on air; give 15 L/min non-rebreather to reach 100%.
traps.trap: Maximal oxygen for hypoxaemia.
traps.fix: Controlled O₂ (Venturi 24–28%) targeting SpO₂ 88–92%; high FiO₂ worsens hypercapnia (V/Q mismatch, Haldane effect).

traps.stem: Bilateral infiltrates with P/F 150 and PCWP 22 mmHg after massive IV fluids.
traps.trap: ARDS – the P/F ratio fits.
traps.fix: Raised filling pressures and fluid overload suggest hydrostatic (cardiogenic) pulmonary oedema; Berlin requires that oedema is not fully explained by heart failure/fluid overload.

cards.text: Berlin ARDS severity (PEEP ≥5): mild P/F {{c1::200–300}}, moderate {{c2::100–200}}, severe {{c3::≤100}}.
Lung-protective ventilation: tidal volume {{c1::6 mL/kg predicted body weight}} and plateau pressure ≤{{c2::30 cmH₂O}}.

cards.front: Which ARDS intervention showed a mortality benefit for P/F <150 in PROSEVA?
cards.back: Prone positioning for ≥16 h/day early in severe ARDS.

cards.front: High peak but normal plateau pressure on the ventilator – what is the problem?
cards.back: Increased airway resistance: bronchospasm, secretions, kinked or bitten tube.

cards.text: NIV is indicated in COPD exacerbation when pH is ≤{{c1::7.35}} with PaCO₂ >{{c2::45 mmHg}} despite medical therapy.

cards.front: Which hypoxaemia mechanism does not correct with 100% oxygen?
cards.back: True shunt (e.g., ARDS, consolidation, intracardiac right-to-left shunt).

title: Pulmonary embolism & DVT work-up; pleural fluid analysis
subject: Medicine
anchor: Sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxia, risk factor (surgery, immobility, cancer, OCP) → PE: pretest probability decides D-dimer vs CTPA
Hypotension (SBP <90 for ≥15 min) or arrest from PE = high-risk (massive) → systemic thrombolysis
Pleural effusion: Light's criteria separate exudate from transudate; low glucose, high ADA, pH, TG, amylase narrow the cause
algorithm:
Suspected PE → haemodynamically stable?
  Unstable (SBP <90 / shock / arrest) → bedside echo (RV dilatation) → UFH + systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg over 2 h)
    lysis contraindicated/failed → surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy
  Stable → clinical probability (Wells / revised Geneva)
    Low (gestalt <15%) → PERC: all 8 negative → no test
    PE unlikely (Wells ≤4) → D-dimer (age-adjusted: age × 10 µg/L if >50 y) → normal = PE excluded; raised → CTPA
    PE likely (Wells >4) → CTPA directly (start anticoagulation while waiting)
    CTPA contraindicated (renal failure, contrast allergy) / pregnancy with normal CXR → V/Q scan
  Confirmed → risk stratify (sPESI, RV dysfunction, troponin)
    Intermediate-high (RV strain + troponin, normotensive) → anticoagulate, monitor, rescue lysis if deteriorates
    Anticoagulation: DOAC (apixaban/rivaroxaban) preferred; LMWH in pregnancy; warfarin in antiphospholipid syndrome
    Provoked → 3 months; unprovoked → ≥3 months, consider extended

tables.title: Wells score for PE
head: Item
Points
rows: PE is the most likely diagnosis
Immobilisation ≥3 days or surgery in previous 4 weeks
≤4 PE unlikely → D-dimer; >4 PE likely → CTPA

tables.title: Pleural fluid clues
head: Finding
Think of
rows: Light's: fluid/serum protein >0.5, fluid/serum LDH >0.6, or fluid LDH >⅔ upper normal serum LDH (any one)
Serum–pleural albumin gradient >1.2 g/dL in a 'Light's exudate' on diuretics
Empyema/complicated parapneumonic, rheumatoid (very low, <30), TB, malignancy, oesophageal rupture, lupus

points: **PERC** (use only when pretest probability is low): age <50, HR <100, SpO₂ ≥95%, no haemoptysis, no oestrogen use, no prior DVT/PE, no unilateral leg swelling, no surgery/trauma needing hospitalisation in last 4 weeks
**D-dimer** is sensitive but non-specific – useful only to **rule out** in low/unlikely probability; never in high probability
**CTPA** = investigation of choice; **V/Q** in renal failure/contrast allergy and often in pregnancy (normal CXR); compression ultrasound for DVT
Commonest ECG finding in PE = **sinus tachycardia**; S1Q3T3 is classic but uncommon
CXR signs: **Westermark** (focal oligaemia), **Hampton hump** (peripheral wedge infarct), **Fleischner** (enlarged pulmonary artery), **Palla** sign
Echo: RV dilatation, **McConnell sign** (RV free-wall hypokinesia with apical sparing)
Commonest cause of pleural effusion = **congestive heart failure** (transudate); commonest exudate = **parapneumonic**
Rheumatoid effusion: very low glucose, low pH, high LDH, cholesterol crystals; **TB effusion**: lymphocytic exudate, ADA >40 U/L, few mesothelial cells (<5%) – pleural biopsy shows granulomas
Empyema/complicated parapneumonic (pus, positive Gram stain/culture, pH <7.2, glucose <60) → **intercostal drainage**

traps.stem: Post-op day 5, sudden dyspnoea, HR 120, Wells 7.5. Order D-dimer first?
traps.trap: D-dimer first – it is the screening test for PE.
traps.fix: With PE likely (Wells >4) go straight to CTPA (and start anticoagulation); a normal D-dimer cannot exclude PE in high probability, and post-op D-dimer is almost always raised.

traps.stem: Normotensive PE with RV dilatation and raised troponin.
traps.trap: Thrombolyse – RV strain means massive PE.
traps.fix: That is intermediate-high risk (submassive). Anticoagulate and monitor; systemic lysis only if haemodynamic decompensation (PEITHO: lysis increased major bleeding/stroke).

traps.stem: CHF patient on furosemide: pleural protein ratio 0.55 (exudate by Light's).
traps.trap: Exudate → tap for malignancy/TB.
traps.fix: Diuretics concentrate pleural protein; check serum–effusion albumin gradient >1.2 g/dL → transudate from heart failure.

cards.text: Light's criteria: exudate if pleural/serum protein >{{c1::0.5}}, pleural/serum LDH >{{c2::0.6}}, or pleural LDH >{{c3::2/3}} of the upper normal serum LDH.
Wells score >{{c1::4}} = PE likely → {{c2::CTPA}}; ≤4 = PE unlikely → {{c3::D-dimer}}.

cards.front: Massive (high-risk) PE definition and treatment?
cards.back: SBP <90 mmHg for ≥15 min (or fall ≥40 mmHg, needing vasopressors, or arrest) due to PE → systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg over 2 h) unless contraindicated.

cards.front: Very low pleural glucose (<30 mg/dL) with high LDH, low pH and RA factor?
cards.back: Rheumatoid pleural effusion.

cards.text: Pleural ADA above {{c1::40 U/L}} in a {{c2::lymphocytic}} exudate supports tuberculous pleuritis.

cards.front: Commonest ECG finding in pulmonary embolism?
cards.back: Sinus tachycardia (S1Q3T3 is classic but seen in a minority).

images.caption: CTPA: filling defect straddling the bifurcation of the main pulmonary artery = saddle embolus

title: Pneumonia, ILD, sarcoidosis, bronchiectasis, lung cancer & flow–volume loops
subject: Medicine
anchor: CAP severity = CURB-65 (Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, RR ≥30, BP <90/≤60, age ≥65): 0–1 home, 2 admit, ≥3 severe
Elderly smoker with basal 'velcro' crackles, clubbing, honeycombing → IPF (UIP pattern); young woman with BHL + erythema nodosum → sarcoidosis (Löfgren)
Central tumour + hyponatraemia/Cushingoid/LEMS → small cell; central + hypercalcaemia → squamous; peripheral in non-smoker → adenocarcinoma

tables.title: Lung cancer types
head: Type
Location / clue
Paraneoplastic / marker
rows: Peripheral; women, non-smokers; EGFR, ALK, ROS1 targets
Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy, Trousseau migratory thrombophlebitis
Central; very smoking-linked; early metastasis; treated with chemo-radiation
SIADH, ectopic ACTH, LEMS, anti-Hu encephalomyelitis, cerebellar degeneration; chromogranin, synaptophysin, CD56

tables.title: Flow–volume loops
head: Pattern
Loop shape
Examples
rows: Narrow, tall 'witch's hat'; normal/↑ FEV1/FVC, ↓ TLC

points: Commonest CAP organism: **S. pneumoniae** (lobar, rusty sputum). **Mycoplasma**: young, cold agglutinins (anti-I IgM), bullous myringitis, erythema multiforme
**Legionella**: high fever with relative bradycardia, diarrhoea, **hyponatraemia**, deranged LFTs; urinary antigen (serogroup 1), BCYE agar; treat macrolide/fluoroquinolone

**Klebsiella**: alcoholics, currant-jelly sputum, upper-lobe cavitation, bulging fissure; **S. aureus**: post-influenza, pneumatoceles; aspiration in supine patient → posterior segment of upper lobe/superior segment of lower lobe (right)
**UIP (IPF)**: subpleural, basal reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis, temporal heterogeneity with fibroblastic foci; antifibrotics **pirfenidone, nintedanib**; steroids harmful
**NSIP**: uniform (temporally homogeneous) ground-glass with subpleural sparing; linked to connective tissue disease (scleroderma); steroid-responsive, better prognosis

Upper-lobe fibrosis: sarcoidosis, silicosis, coal workers', TB, ankylosing spondylitis, chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis; lower-lobe: IPF, asbestosis, CTD, drugs (amiodarone, bleomycin, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin)

**Sarcoidosis**: non-caseating granulomas, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, ↑ ACE, hypercalcaemia (macrophage 1α-hydroxylase), BAL CD4:CD8 >3.5; **Löfgren** (BHL + erythema nodosum + ankle arthritis + fever, good prognosis); **Heerfordt** (uveitis, parotid swelling, facial palsy, fever)

**Bronchiectasis** HRCT: **signet-ring sign** (bronchus wider than adjacent artery), tram-tracks, no tapering; post-infective (incl. TB) commonest in India; CF → upper lobes; ABPA → central bronchiectasis; Kartagener → situs inversus + sinusitis + infertility (dynein arm defect)

**DLCO**: ↓ in emphysema, ILD, PE, pulmonary hypertension, anaemia; ↑ in asthma, alveolar haemorrhage, polycythaemia, left-to-right shunt; normal in chronic bronchitis and chest-wall/neuromuscular restriction
**Pancoast tumour** (superior sulcus): shoulder/arm pain in C8–T1, Horner syndrome; SVC syndrome commonest malignant cause = small cell carcinoma

traps.stem: Pneumonia in a 70-year-old: confused, urea 9 mmol/L, RR 24, BP 120/80.
traps.trap: CURB-65 = 2 (confusion, urea) – ward admission.
traps.fix: Count age ≥65 as well: confusion + urea + age = 3 → severe CAP, consider HDU/ICU.

traps.stem: Flow–volume loop: plateau on both inspiration and expiration in a patient extubated after 3 weeks of ventilation.
traps.trap: Restrictive lung disease – reduced flows.
traps.fix: Fixed upper airway obstruction (post-intubation tracheal stenosis): flattening of BOTH limbs; restrictive loops are narrow but keep a normal shape.

traps.stem: IPF patient worsening; start high-dose prednisolone + azathioprine?
traps.trap: Steroid-based immunosuppression for fibrosis.
traps.fix: PANTHER-IPF showed harm with prednisone + azathioprine + NAC; use antifibrotics (pirfenidone or nintedanib), O₂, pulmonary rehab, transplant referral.

cards.text: CURB-65: Confusion, Urea >{{c1::7 mmol/L}}, Respiratory rate ≥{{c2::30}}, BP systolic <90 or diastolic ≤60, age ≥{{c3::65}}.

cards.front: Flattened inspiratory limb only on flow–volume loop?
cards.back: Variable extrathoracic upper airway obstruction (e.g., vocal cord paralysis).

cards.text: Small cell lung cancer paraneoplastic syndromes: {{c1::SIADH}}, {{c2::ectopic ACTH}} and {{c3::Lambert–Eaton}} syndrome.

cards.front: UIP vs NSIP on HRCT?
cards.back: UIP: basal subpleural reticulation, honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis, heterogeneous. NSIP: uniform ground-glass with subpleural sparing; CTD-associated; better prognosis.

cards.front: Löfgren syndrome?
cards.back: Acute sarcoidosis: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy + erythema nodosum + ankle periarthritis + fever – good prognosis, often self-limiting.

cards.text: Legionella pneumonia classically causes {{c1::hyponatraemia}} and is diagnosed rapidly by {{c2::urinary antigen}} testing.

title: Shock haemodynamics & Sepsis-3 management
subject: Medicine
anchor: Sepsis = infection + acute organ dysfunction (SOFA rise ≥2); septic shock = vasopressor needed for MAP ≥65 AND lactate >2 mmol/L despite fluids
Warm peripheries + low SVR + high CO = distributive; cold, clammy + high SVR + low CO = hypovolaemic/cardiogenic/obstructive
Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, norepinephrine
algorithm:
Suspected sepsis → within 1 hour (SSC hour-1 bundle):
  Measure lactate (repeat if >2 mmol/L)
  Blood cultures before antibiotics (do not delay antibiotics)
  Broad-spectrum antibiotics (≤1 h if shock or probable sepsis; ≤3 h if sepsis only possible and no shock)
  Hypotension or lactate ≥4 → 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid within 3 h
  MAP <65 during/after fluids → norepinephrine (peripheral start acceptable)
    NE 0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min → add vasopressin 0.03 U/min
    NE ≥0.25 µg/kg/min for ≥4 h → hydrocortisone 200 mg/day
    Cardiac dysfunction with hypoperfusion → add dobutamine (or switch to adrenaline)
  Source control (drain abscess, remove infected line) as soon as practical
  Reassess with dynamic measures, capillary refill, lactate clearance

tables.title: SIRS vs qSOFA vs SOFA
head: Tool
Components
Use
rows: T >38 or <36 °C; HR >90; RR >20 or PaCO₂ <32; WBC >12,000, <4,000 or >10% bands
Bedside prognostic flag – SSC 2021 advises NOT to use alone for screening
PaO₂/FiO₂, platelets, bilirubin, MAP/vasopressors, GCS, creatinine/urine output (each 0–4)

points: **Sepsis-3 (2016)**: 'life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection'; 'severe sepsis' term abandoned
**Norepinephrine** = first-line vasopressor in septic shock; target **MAP ≥65 mmHg**; dopamine only in selected bradycardic patients
**Balanced crystalloids** (Ringer lactate) preferred over 0.9% saline; albumin if large volumes needed; **avoid starches** (HES → AKI)
Neurogenic shock (cord injury above T6): **hypotension + bradycardia + warm skin** → fluids, norepinephrine/phenylephrine, atropine for bradycardia
**Anaphylaxis**: IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) in anterolateral thigh, repeat every 5 min; IV adrenaline only by experienced hands/refractory
Cardiogenic shock: commonest cause is acute MI with LV failure → urgent revascularisation; inotrope dobutamine, NE if hypotensive; mechanical support
**Shock index** (HR/SBP) >1 suggests significant shock; lactate >4 mmol/L = marker of severe hypoperfusion
SvO₂/ScvO₂ is **high** in sepsis (impaired O₂ extraction) but **low** in hypovolaemic/cardiogenic shock (high extraction)

traps.stem: Septic shock, MAP 58 after 2 L crystalloid. First pressor?
traps.trap: Dopamine – classic 'renal dose' inotrope.
traps.fix: Norepinephrine is first-line; dopamine causes more arrhythmias and no renal protection. Add vasopressin if NE requirement rises.

traps.stem: Spinal cord injury at C6, BP 80/40, HR 48, warm dry skin.
traps.trap: Haemorrhagic shock – transfuse.
traps.fix: Neurogenic shock (loss of sympathetic tone): hypotension with bradycardia and warm skin. Exclude bleeding, then fluids + vasopressor (± atropine). Haemorrhagic shock gives tachycardia and cold skin.

traps.stem: Patient with infection, qSOFA 1 but SOFA increase of 3 points.
traps.trap: Not sepsis because qSOFA is <2.
traps.fix: Sepsis is defined by an acute SOFA rise ≥2 due to infection; qSOFA is only a prognostic bedside prompt, not a diagnostic criterion.

cards.text: Septic shock (Sepsis-3) = vasopressors to keep MAP ≥{{c1::65 mmHg}} AND serum lactate >{{c2::2 mmol/L}} despite adequate fluid resuscitation.
qSOFA: respiratory rate ≥{{c1::22}}, altered mentation, systolic BP ≤{{c2::100 mmHg}}.

cards.front: Cardiogenic vs hypovolaemic shock on PA catheter?
cards.back: Both: low CO, high SVR. Cardiogenic: high PCWP and CVP. Hypovolaemic: low PCWP and CVP.

cards.front: Septic shock haemodynamics?
cards.back: High/normal CO, low SVR, low/normal PCWP, high ScvO₂ (warm shock).

cards.text: Hour-1 bundle fluid bolus: {{c1::30 mL/kg}} crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥{{c2::4 mmol/L}}.

cards.front: When to add hydrocortisone in septic shock?
cards.back: Ongoing norepinephrine (or adrenaline) ≥0.25 µg/kg/min for ≥4 h – IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (SSC 2021).

verify: Sepsis-3 (JAMA 2016); Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 adult guideline; hour-1 bundle (SSC 2018).

title: Anaemia basics: microcytic work-up, B12 vs folate, haemolysis labs
subject: Medicine
anchor: Microcytic anaemia → ferritin first: low = iron deficiency; normal/high → ACD, thalassaemia trait (Hb electrophoresis/HPLC), sideroblastic (marrow ring sideroblasts)
Macrocytic + hypersegmented neutrophils = megaloblastic: MMA ↑ only in B12 deficiency; homocysteine ↑ in both
↑ LDH + ↑ unconjugated bilirubin + ↓ haptoglobin + reticulocytosis = haemolysis → DAT (Coombs) next

tables.title: Microcytic anaemia: iron studies
head: Test
Iron deficiency
Anaemia of chronic disease
β-thalassaemia trait
Sideroblastic
rows: Ring sideroblasts (Prussian blue); basophilic stippling in lead

tables.title: B12 vs folate deficiency
head: Feature
Vitamin B12
Folate
rows: Subacute combined degeneration (posterior + lateral columns), neuropathy, dementia
Pernicious anaemia, gastrectomy, ileal resection/Crohn's, strict vegan, metformin, PPIs, D. latum, blind loop
Poor diet, alcohol, pregnancy, haemolysis, methotrexate, phenytoin, trimethoprim
IM hydroxo/cyanocobalamin 1000 µg; correct B12 before or with folate

points: **Serum ferritin** is the single best test for iron deficiency (falls first – stores deplete before serum iron); bone marrow iron (Prussian blue) is the gold standard
Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant: inflammation can mask iron deficiency → use a higher ferritin cut-off or transferrin saturation/sTfR
Response to iron: **reticulocytosis in 5–10 days**; Hb rises ~1–2 g/dL every 2–3 weeks; continue iron ~3 months after Hb normalises to refill stores
**Mentzer index** = MCV/RBC count: <13 thalassaemia trait, >13 iron deficiency
Sideroblastic causes: X-linked *ALAS2*, alcohol, **isoniazid** (B6), lead, copper deficiency, MDS (ring sideroblasts ≥15% of erythroblasts)
**Pernicious anaemia**: anti-intrinsic factor antibody (specific) and anti-parietal cell antibody (sensitive); atrophic gastritis of body/fundus, ↑ gastrin, ↑ gastric cancer/carcinoid risk
Giving **folate alone** in B12 deficiency corrects the blood picture but allows neurological damage to progress
Intravascular haemolysis: haemoglobinaemia, **haemoglobinuria**, **haemosiderinuria**, very low haptoglobin, schistocytes (MAHA); extravascular: spherocytes, splenomegaly
**Warm AIHA** (IgG, extravascular, spherocytes; SLE, CLL, methyldopa) → steroids; **cold agglutinin** (IgM + C3, Mycoplasma, EBV) → avoid cold, rituximab

**G6PD deficiency**: X-linked, oxidant trigger (primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, fava beans); **Heinz bodies** & **bite cells**; enzyme assay may be falsely normal during acute haemolysis

traps.stem: Microcytic anaemia, Hb 10, RBC 6.1 million/µL, ferritin normal, RDW normal.
traps.trap: Iron deficiency – start oral iron.
traps.fix: Thalassaemia trait: high RBC count, normal RDW, Mentzer <13, normal ferritin → HPLC (HbA2 >3.5%). Iron is useless and harmful long-term.

traps.stem: Macrocytic anaemia with ataxia and loss of vibration sense; folate low-normal. Start folic acid?
traps.trap: Folate replacement because folate is borderline.
traps.fix: Neurology = B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration). Check B12/MMA and give IM B12 first; folate alone can worsen neurological damage.

traps.stem: Haemolysis after primaquine; G6PD assay on day 2 is normal.
traps.trap: G6PD deficiency excluded.
traps.fix: Young RBCs/reticulocytes (high G6PD) dominate after acute haemolysis → false normal. Repeat the assay ~2–3 months later or use a quantitative test with reticulocyte correction.

cards.text: Raised methylmalonic acid with raised homocysteine indicates {{c1::vitamin B12}} deficiency; raised homocysteine with normal MMA indicates {{c2::folate}} deficiency.
Iron deficiency iron profile: ferritin {{c1::↓}}, TIBC {{c2::↑}}, transferrin saturation {{c3::↓}}.

cards.front: Anaemia of chronic disease – central mechanism?
cards.back: Hepcidin ↑ (IL-6 driven) → ferroportin degraded → iron trapped in macrophages and poorly absorbed: low iron, low TIBC, normal/high ferritin.

cards.front: Hallmark labs of haemolysis?
cards.back: ↑ LDH, ↑ unconjugated bilirubin, ↓ haptoglobin, ↑ reticulocytes; intravascular adds haemoglobinuria & haemosiderinuria.

cards.text: Mentzer index (MCV ÷ RBC count) <{{c1::13}} suggests {{c2::thalassaemia trait}}.

cards.front: Earliest marker to fall in developing iron deficiency?
cards.back: Serum ferritin (depletion of stores) – before serum iron, transferrin saturation or Hb fall.

images.caption: Iron deficiency: microcytic hypochromic RBCs with wide central pallor and pencil cells (MCV 55 fL)
Hypersegmented neutrophils (≥6 lobes, or >5% with 5 lobes) – megaloblastic anaemia (B12/folate deficiency)
Schistocytes (fragmented RBCs) – intravascular microangiopathic haemolysis (here HUS; also TTP, DIC)
